n: In spring, Joab besieges Rabbah, Ammon’s capital, while David stays in Jerusalem. 2 Samuel tells us this is when David sinned with Bathsheba; the chronicler leaves that story out, focusing on David’s role in God’s plan rather than repeating his failures.

f.w: at the time that kings go out to battle
f.g: Spring, after the rainy season, when armies could travel.

n: David takes the crown from the Ammonite king—or from their god Milcom—weighing about seventy-five pounds and set with a precious stone, and much plunder.

f.g: Hebrew malkam; can also be read as “Milcom,” the Ammonite god, whose idol may have worn the crown.
About 75 pounds (34 kg)—likely worn only briefly or ceremonially.

n: David puts the Ammonite people to work with saws, iron picks and axes—hard labor for the conquered. Older translations read it as torture, but many scholars favor forced labor.

f.g: The Hebrew can mean “set them to work at saws”; compare 2 Samuel 12:31.
Heavy tools with iron teeth for breaking up ground.

n: War breaks out again with the Philistines, and Sibbechai kills a descendant of the giants. The Philistines are subdued.

f.g: Descendants of the Rapha, a race of very tall warriors.

n: Elhanan kills Lahmi, brother of Goliath, whose spear was as thick as a weaver’s beam. This clarifies 2 Samuel 21:19, which, as copied, seems to say Elhanan killed Goliath himself.

f.g: The thick wooden rod on a loom—a very heavy spear shaft.

n: At Gath, a huge man with six fingers and six toes on each hand and foot is another descendant of the giants.
When he taunts Israel, as Goliath once had, David’s nephew Jonathan kills him.
These giants of Gath fell to David and his men. What once terrified Israel in the days of Moses and Saul is overcome by faith in God.

f.w: they fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants
